name: Mushafi
bio: The book says Mushafi belonged to a distinguished family of Amroha, lived at first at Lucknow and then went to Delhi, where he held famous literary reunions at which gathered many poets of whom he was the inspirer and teacher.

The 2 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poems.title: I, like a wandering bubble
poems.author: Mushafi
poems.translator: trans. Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1919)
poems.text:
I, like a wandering bubble,
    Am blown here and there
Shifting and changing and fashioned
    Of water and air.

Thou turnest thy face, O Beloved,
    I cannot tell why,
Art thou shy of a mirror, Beloved?
    Thy mirror am I!

When over her face she unloosened
    The dusk of her hair,
What need had the world of the cloud-wreaths,
    They fled in despair.

poems.title: No man hath ever passed
poems.author: Mushafi
poems.translator: trans. Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1919)
poems.text:
No man hath ever passed
    Into the Country of Eternal Rest
        With every longing stilled.
Who hath not lingering cast
    Long looks behind, and in his eager breast
        Held many a secret yearning unfulfilled?

Ah, Mushafi, to thee
    Silence and thought in solitude are best,
        For thou hast known
That laurel crowns are idle vanity;
    There is no worldly rank thou covetest,
        And what to thee is Suleiman's high throne?
